[h1]The Operator – Review[/h1]
I’ve just finished my first playthrough of [i]The Operator[/i], and it really got under my skin. At first, it feels like a clear throwback to [i]Orwell[/i] — digging through files, connecting clues, and sitting with that constant, uneasy sense of surveillance. The retro desktop setup is spot-on and makes the whole thing feel strangely real. About halfway through, I started wondering if the game itself was testing me. Was I part of the experiment? That thought stuck with me right to the end. The puzzles are clever and rewarding, and the story ramps up quickly, leaving you with plenty to think about. I’m already planning another run to see what I missed.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]What Holds It Back[/h2]
That said, the biggest drawback is its length. At around three to four hours, it ends just as you’re fully immersed. I couldn’t help but think how much more replayable it could be with a few extra systems layered on top.
[list]
[*]Randomised agents
[*]Modular or shuffled case fragments
[*]Overlapping investigative threads across multiple cases
[/list]
Something like that would fit perfectly with the game’s investigative tone and make it feel less like a one-and-done experience. Piecing together evidence that changes each run would add a lot of longevity.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Similar Games Worth Mentioning[/h2]
If you enjoyed [i]Orwell[/i] or [i]Her Story[/i], you’ll feel right at home here. That said, if you’re looking for longer playtime, there are other options worth considering:
[list]
[*][b]Orwell[/b] – branching choices across multiple episodes
[*][b]Return of the Obra Dinn[/b] – a sprawling mystery with dozens of characters
[*][b]The Case of the Golden Idol[/b] – interconnected cases with deep logic puzzles
[*][b]Cyber Manhunt[/b] – hacking and social engineering-driven investigations
[*][b]Shadows of Doubt[/b] – a procedural detective sandbox with near-infinite replayability
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
This is a short, sharp, and stylish thriller that absolutely nails its atmosphere and narrative hooks. It’s not perfect — some dialogue feels stiff, and the illusion of choice can occasionally be frustrating — but for a few hours of tense, thought‑provoking gameplay, it’s absolutely worth it. I just hope a possible sequel takes the next step and gives us the freedom to dig deeper, for longer.

[b]Recommendation:[/b] [u]Recommended[/u]

The Operator is an incredibly immersive experience that makes you feel fully absorbed in its world from the very beginning. The gameplay does an excellent job of pulling you into the role, with interfaces and mechanics that feel natural and believable. Combined with a strong, well-paced storyline, the game constantly keeps you engaged and curious, making every discovery feel impactful.

The only real issue is that it left me wanting more - not because it was lacking, but because the detective-style gameplay was so enjoyable. I genuinely wished there was more time spent investigating, analyzing information, and digging deeper into cases. That desire for more content is ultimately a compliment to how compelling the experience is. The Operator delivers a memorable, story-driven journey, and it’s the kind of game that makes you hope for future expansions or sequels just so you can spend more time doing what it does so well.

Ok, now the main thing that got me really angry. Spoilers ahead, if you want to experience the story for yourself, stop reading.



You are Evan Tanner, an FBI Operator, assisting field agents by searching through files and coordinating stuff. Your first case is a murder where a man named Jenkins was shot, and a list with a bunch of names is found. The weird thing: one of the names was censored, but only after the document got secured as evidence, so theres some shady cover-up shit happening inside of the FBI.
Then, you get contacted by HAL (Alice Truman), a wanted hacker, who needs your help with uncovering said shady shit. Later, Jenkins killer gets shot by a mysterious bold man who is in no database.

A bunch of shit happens, and you find out about a biomedical company named BioM, lead by Jenkins, whose target it is to create a drug that can erase memories. Jenkins intention is to make it possible to erase trauma from peoples memories (his daughter (probably) took her life because she got traumatized or something idk and then his wife killed herself as well...). However, the funding comes from some shadow-world-government people who intend to use the drug to erase peoples minds and rewrite their memories. Spoiler: You are one of those. You are a double agent, sent to win HALs trust. But you don't know that, since your objective is deeply burried inside of your mind.
In the end, you and HAL (and some others) try to find out who the double-agent in the FBI is by infiltrating the server room. However, the hitman from earlier, who got caught at some point in the story (irrelevant) is freed by said double-agent and shoots some people. You try to escapa but get shot. Everything is covered up as you being the double-agent (which si partially true because you ARE one, but not THE one) and all your friends get shot or jailed. HAL, who gives you her identity, is compromised since you ,remeber, are a double agent, so you somehow redirect that information to the hitman guy or the shadow government or idk who the fuck but basically it was all a huge trap to infiltrate the possible resistance that could pose a threat to said shadow government. You and all your friends die and all of your actions were meaningless. THE END.

First of all, let me say that this is a good final product if you see it as a mildly interactive visual novel.

The art direction is great, with the soundscape, voice acting, graphics and beats creating the right atmosphere for a conspiracy thriller.

The problem with it is that it's not a Game. It's a linear railroad that drives you from action to action where you can perform simple, easy puzzles. You don't have any agency, and in most places there is no possibility for branching the story.

Even with a fixed outcome, the developers could have done more with script to give some illusion of agency. The most annoying part is that for every dialog, no matter what is your choice, the outcome of that interaction always the same.

So, play it if you want to watch a conspiracy story with some CSI-type procedural puzzles in the mix.

Avoid if you want to play a game with a minimum of agency.

This was such a frustrating experience. 
The core gameplay, working as an FDI operator, is very engaging and interesting. Solving the cases, using the tools at your disposal and communicating with agents voiced by real actors was great. I could have done that for hours on end.
The story, however, was abysmal. Riddled with clichés and TV tropes, easy to figure out from the introductory sequence and you felt railroaded down the storyline at every turn with your choices hardly mattering.
Worst of all, after 2-3 hours of playtime (right outside the refund window) the game just ends. Just as the world seemed to be opening up, it just ends.

You can feel the amount of work put into this, but its simply not worth the price to play what felt to be a prologue to a real game.

Reluctant thumbs up, mostly for the uniqueness of concept. Basically you're the assistant the main character has in typical video games. The tactical support on the radio rather the one in the field. The game presents you with this role well, the art direction and controls are solid, and it's immersive

The plot is unfortunately totally railroaded, with no meaningful decisions to make, only concequences for failing some puzzles. There is only one ending, and that's very lame since: 1) its tone qualifies as a neutral or bad ending in the games that have such a concept, and 2) It would have taken them like a day to cook up some alternative graphics in the ending slideshow, to give us a good ending as a reward for doing well in the game!

Be aware that it's a very short experience. I finished in 4 hours and I wasn't rushing at all. I spent time poking for hidden depths and didn't get any reward for it. So, get it on sale!
